# Backtesting System Architecture

Oct 2, 2026 · @qiwen

## Overview

The system has 8 layers that talk to each other only through events. It targets mid- to low- frequency long-options strategies (holding periods of days to weeks), while the core stays asset-agnostic so stocks, ETFs and futures run on the same engine.

Five principles apply to every layer:

1. One-way dependencies: a layer depends only on interfaces defined below it.
2. Correctness by mechanism: look-ahead, illegal trades and accounting errors are blocked by the foundation, not by the strategy author's discipline.
3. Same code for backtest and live: strategy, portfolio and risk components run unchanged in both.
4. Pessimistic by default: fills, costs and capacity err toward understating returns. For options, that means paying the spread.
5. Reproducible: config, code version and data version uniquely determine a run's result.

Options differ from stocks in three ways, and each layer below reflects them:

- The tradable set changes every day. Contracts list and expire, so the universe is an option chain, not a ticker list.
- Price has more dimensions. Spot, implied volatility and time all move the price, so risk is measured in Greeks.
- Costs are dominated by the bid-ask spread and time decay, not by commissions.

> **Diagram, page 2 of the source PDF** — *System architecture · 8 layers, event-driven*
>
> Not reproduced in this conversion; see `Plan/backtest-system-architecture.pdf`, page 2.

The main path runs top-down: data → signals → portfolio and risk → execution → accounting. Positions and cash flow back read-only to the signal and portfolio layers, and the engine drives the processing order.

## Strategy Model: Seven Components

The strategy is defined by seven components that follow a trade from setup to exit. This section fixes only their structure: where each one sits, when it runs, what it can read and what it can emit. The internal logic and form of each component are not decided yet; each is an empty slot that any variant can fill and that can be researched, swapped or tuned on its own.

> **Diagram, page 3 of the source PDF** — *Trade lifecycle · 4 states, 7 components*
>
> Not reproduced in this conversion; see `Plan/backtest-system-architecture.pdf`, page 3.

A trade waits in Idle until Setup / Regime arms it, opens when Entry fires and Positioning sizes it, and is managed each period by Take Profit, Stop Loss, Headwind and Hedge until it closes. The order in which those four run is a lifecycle setting, not yet decided.

### Lifecycle states

| State | Scope | Entered when | Component slots that run |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Idle | Candidate (one per underlying) | No valid setup | 1 Setup / Regime |
| Armed | Candidate (one per underlying) | Setup / Regime marks the candidate as ready; returns to Idle when the setup is no longer valid | 1 Setup / Regime, 2 Entry, then 6 Positioning when Entry fires |
| Open | Trade (one per trade_id) | First fill received; the candidate's setup context is copied into the new trade | 3 Take Profit, 4 Stop Loss, 5 Headwind, 7 Hedge / Protection, every snapshot |
| Closed | Trade (one per trade_id) | Position fully exited or expired | None; the record is finalized and shadow tracking starts (see 5.2) |

Setups belong to the underlying and trades belong to a trade_id. One candidate can therefore produce several trades over time, and whether it may hold more than one at once is a lifecycle setting.

Lifecycle settings are left open on purpose. They live in the lifecycle config, not inside any component, so they can be researched like the components themselves:

| Setting | Question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| open_state_order | In what order do slots 3, 4, 5 and 7 run each snapshot? |
| conflict_policy | How are conflicting actions in the same snapshot resolved? |
| max_concurrent_trades | How many open trades may one underlying hold at once? |
| reentry_policy | When may a candidate arm again after a trade closes? |
| check_frequency | At which snapshots do the Open-state slots run? It must match live trading exactly; no intra-snapshot stop or target fills are assumed |

### Component contracts

The table below is the default wiring for each slot: the level it works at, when it is evaluated, the data it reads, the actions it can emit and what it writes to the context. These are defaults to start from; any of them can be changed, and what a slot does with its inputs is left to its variants.

| Slot | Level | Evaluated | Reads (default) | Emits | Writes to context |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Setup / Regime | Underlying (candidate) | Each snapshot while Idle or Armed | Underlying price history (completed bars plus the current snapshot), realized volatility, ATM IV, IV rank (rolling), term structure, skew, event calendar, regime features | Arm or disarm the candidate | State, reference levels, score, regime label |
| 2 Entry | Underlying, then contracts | Each snapshot while Armed | Underlying snapshot, setup context, option chain (quotes, IV, Greeks, spread, open interest, days to expiry) | OPEN with legs, or nothing | Trigger, reference price, IV and Greeks at entry |
| 6 Positioning | Trade within the book | When OPEN or ADD is issued, or REDUCE needs a quantity | Setup score, entry context, premium budget, book premium at risk, book Greeks, liquidity caps (displayed size, volume) | Contract quantities | Quantity, budget used |
| 3 Take Profit | Trade | Each snapshot while Open | Premium P&L, underlying versus setup and entry reference levels, MFE, days to expiry, Greeks, IV change since entry | REDUCE, CLOSE, SET_STOP, request HEDGE_ADD, HOLD | Levels reached |
| 4 Stop Loss | Trade | Each snapshot while Open | Premium P&L, underlying versus setup and entry reference levels, MAE, time in trade, IV change | CLOSE, REDUCE, HOLD | Active stop level, trigger |
| 5 Headwind (trade) | Trade | Each snapshot while Open | Changes since entry: regime label, IV, theta and days to expiry, delta, spread and liquidity, upcoming events; other slots' context | REDUCE, CLOSE, ROLL, SET_STOP, request HEDGE_ADD, HOLD | Active factors, severity |
| 5 Headwind (book) | Book (Layer 3) | Each snapshot | Book Greeks, premium at risk, drawdown, market-wide regime and volatility | Scale, veto or force actions on trades | Outcome written to each affected trade |

> **Diagram, page 6 of the source PDF** — *Component interactions · 7 slots, 1 shared trade context*
>
> Not reproduced in this conversion; see `Plan/backtest-system-architecture.pdf`, page 6.

| Slot | Level | Evaluated | Reads (default) | Emits | Writes to context |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7 Hedge (trade) | Trade | On request, or each snapshot while Open | Trade Greeks and P&L, headwind context, quotes and cost of hedge instruments (underlying shares, index futures, options) | HEDGE_ADD, HEDGE_REMOVE | Hedge legs, hedge cost |
| 7 Hedge (book) | Book (Layer 3) | Each snapshot | Book Greeks, scenario losses, hedge instrument quotes | Hedge legs under a book-level trade_id | Book hedge record |

Every slot reads only through the DataView, so the available_at cut applies to all of them. A variant may read less than its default, or more within the DataView.

### Component interactions

Slots never call each other directly. Every influence between them, and between them and the rest of the system, goes through two structures: a shared trade context and trade actions. Which links a strategy actually uses is decided by its variants, not by the architecture.

The trade context is a per-trade_id record. Setup / Regime writes to a candidate context per underlying, which is copied into the trade context when the trade opens. Each slot
writes only to its own namespace (setup, entry, `take_profit`, `stop_loss`, headwind,

positioning, hedge) and can read all of them, plus read-only book, position and fill information. Every write is timestamped and logged, so research can trace which information reached which decision.

Influence channels between slots

| Channel | Meaning | Mechanism | Possible links (decided per variant) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gate | One slot decides whether another may run | Lifecycle state | Setup / Regime → Entry |
| Pass- through | One slot's output becomes another's input | Written to the trade context, read by later slots | Setup or Entry → Positioning, Take Profit, Stop Loss, Headwind, Hedge |
| Request | One slot asks another to act | A trade action handled by the owning slot (for example HEDGE_ADD by Hedge, ADD or REDUCE quantities by Positioning) | Headwind → Hedge, Stop Loss, Positioning; Take Profit → Hedge |
| Override | Two slots issue conflicting actions in the same period | Conflict policy in the lifecycle config | Any of the Open-state slots |
| Shared context | Market state visible to every slot | Regime and other features in the DataView | Setup / Regime features → any slot |

Links between slots and the rest of the system

| Direction | Through | What it changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slots → Signals output | Trade actions → SignalCombiner → SignalEvent | What the strategy wants to do this period |
| Portfolio and risk → slots | Constraint, RiskRule, book-wide Headwind and Hedge | Scale, veto or force actions; the outcome (for example “vetoed by premium limit”) is written back to the trade context so slots can see it |
| Execution → slots | Fill and order status | Trade context records fills, partial fills and rejects; lifecycle state changes only on fills (Armed → Open on the first fill) |
| Accounting → slots | Positions, P&L, Greeks, MFE and MAE | What Open-state slots read each period |
| Data → slots | DataView, cut at available_at | All market information a slot can use |
| Engine → slots | Lifecycle state, period timer, expiry events | When each slot runs |

Because slots can depend on each other through these channels, researching one slot in isolation is not always enough. Section 6.3 adds interaction tests for that.

Two practical limits on Hedge: if a variant sells an option leg, Layers 4 and 5 need margin and assignment modeling first; and in the US, delta hedging can use the underlying shares (short sales need a borrow), index futures such as ES and MES, or options, so Layers 4 and 5 must support whichever instruments are chosen.

### Action vocabulary

Every component emits TradeAction events from one shared vocabulary, so all decisions can be logged, compared and attributed the same way:

| Action | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| OPEN | Open a new trade with its legs |
| ADD | Increase an open trade (scale in) |
| REDUCE | Close a fraction of the trade |
| CLOSE | Close the whole trade, hedge legs included |
| ROLL | Replace legs with a later expiry or new strike |
| HEDGE_ADD / HEDGE_REMOVE | Attach or remove protective legs |
| SET_STOP | Move the stop level |
| HOLD | Explicit no-change, logged with the reason |

Each action carries trade_id, component_id, variant version, reason and the data values that triggered it.

### Research hooks per component

| Component | Core question | Research tools that apply (see 6.3) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Setup / Regime | Does gating entries improve results, and in which conditions? | Ablation, variant swap, results split by setup state |
| 2 Entry | Is the entry timing better than random within valid setups? | Random-entry baseline, variant swap, event study |
| 3 Take Profit | Does it lock in gains or cut winners too early? | Counterfactual exits, variant swap, MFE analysis |
| 4 Stop Loss | Does it save more than it costs? | Counterfactual exits, variant swap, MAE analysis |
| 5 Headwind | Which responses to adverse factors help? | Ablation per factor, counterfactual exits, attribution by component |
| 6 Positioning | Does sizing add value beyond trade selection? | Flat-size baseline, variant swap, drawdown comparison |
| 7 Hedge / Protection | Is protection worth its cost? | Ablation, hedge-leg P&L, tail and drawdown comparison |

Every trade records MFE and MAE (maximum favorable and adverse excursion) in both premium and underlying terms. They are the raw material for Take Profit and Stop Loss research.

### Modifying a component

- Every variant is registered by name and version; the config chooses which variant fills each slot and its parameters.
- Changing one slot produces a run that differs from its baseline in that slot alone, so the two results are directly comparable.
- Each variant ships with unit tests on fixed scenarios, so a modified variant cannot silently change behavior elsewhere.

Config skeleton (slots only; variants to be defined):

```yaml
strategy:
  setup:        {variant: tbd, version: tbd, params: {}}
  entry:        {variant: tbd, version: tbd, params: {}}
  take_profit:  {variant: tbd, version: tbd, params: {}}
  stop_loss:    {variant: tbd, version: tbd, params: {}}
  headwind:     {variant: tbd, version: tbd, params: {}}
  positioning:  {variant: tbd, version: tbd, params: {}}
  hedge:        {variant: tbd, version: tbd, params: {}}
  lifecycle:
    open_state_order: tbd        # run order of slots 3, 4, 5, 7
    conflict_policy: tbd         # how same-snapshot conflicts resolve
    max_concurrent_trades: tbd   # per underlying
    reentry_policy: tbd          # when a candidate may arm again
    check_frequency: tbd         # must equal live trading
  timing:
    signal_snapshot: tbd         # e.g. 15:45 ET
    fill_latency: tbd            # e.g. next quote 5 minutes later
```

<a id="section-0"></a>
## Layer 0: Foundation

The foundation defines the contract every layer shares: events, the component interface, time and data visibility, and correctness checks. Fix it first, and the layers above can be built and swapped independently.

<a id="section-0-1"></a>
### 0.1 Events

Events are the only way layers communicate. Every event is immutable and carries a timestamp ts and a sequence number seq for ordering within the same instant.

| Event | Producer | Consumers | Key fields |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MarketEvent (bar) | Data | Signals, Execution, Accounting | symbol, ts, OHLCV, available_at |
| QuoteEvent (snapshot) | Data | Signals, Execution, Accounting | symbol, ts, bid, ask, bid/ask size, last, volume, open interest, available_at |
| CorporateActionEvent | Data | Accounting | type (dividend, split, rights), ex-date, ratio |
| ContractAdjustEvent | Data | Accounting, Signals | contract, old and new multiplier, old and new strike, new code |
| UniverseEvent | Data | Signals | effective date, members (underlyings and listed contracts) |
| TimerEvent | Clock | All layers | start of day, snapshot time, rebalance day, end of day |
| SignalEvent | Signals | Portfolio | trade_id, action (OPEN, REDUCE, CLOSE, ROLL, HEDGE_ADD and others), underlying, legs, fraction, reason, component_id |
| TargetPortfolioEvent | Portfolio | Execution | target quantity per contract, reasons |
| RiskEvent | Portfolio risk | Portfolio, Engine | triggered rule, action (scale down, no new positions, liquidate) |
| OrderEvent | Execution | Matching | order_id, side, quantity, type, limit price, time in force |
| FillEvent | Matching | Accounting | filled quantity, price, fee, slippage, ts |
| OrderStatusEvent | Matching | Portfolio, Logging | partial fill, reject, cancel, and reason |
| ExpiryEvent | Clock | Accounting, Signals | contract, settlement price, exercise or lapse decision |

Processing order within one timestamp is fixed: corporate actions and contract adjustments → market data → signals → portfolio and risk → orders → fills → expiry settlement → accounting → end-of-day snapshot.

<a id="section-0-2"></a>
### 0.2 Component protocol

All replaceable logic implements one base class. A component reads context and affects the system only by returning events. It never mutates the account directly.

```
class Component:
    name: str                 # registry name, referenced from config
    params: ParamSchema       # types, defaults, valid ranges

    def on_start(self, ctx): ...
    def on_event(self, event, ctx) -> list[Event]: ...
    def on_end(self, ctx): ...
    def get_state(self) -> dict: ...   # serializable, for resume
    def set_state(self, state): ...
```

ctx provides clock (current time and calendars), data (the data view), portfolio (positions, cash and Greeks, read-only), logger and config.

| Layer | Component subtypes |
| --- | --- |
| Data | Loader, Validator, Adjuster, FeatureCalculator, RegimeClassifier, IVCalculator, GreeksCalculator, SurfaceBuilder |
| Signals | UniverseSelector, Filter, SetupRule, EntryRule, ContractSelector, StructureBuilder, TakeProfitRule, StopLossRule, HeadwindRule, PositionHedgeRule, RollRule, SignalCombiner |
| Portfolio and risk | RebalanceRule, Sizer (Positioning), Optimizer, Constraint, RiskRule, ScenarioRule, PortfolioHedgeRule |
| Execution | MarketRule, FillModel, SlippageModel, CostModel, ExerciseModel |

Components register by name. The parameter schema drives both config validation and auto-generated web forms.

<a id="section-0-3"></a>
### 0.3 Clock and data view

- Clock: trading calendar (holidays, half days), session phases (opening cross, continuous trading, closing cross) in US Eastern time and the expiry calendar. It is the single source of now.
- DataView(t): returns only data with `available_at ≤ t`. Queries: `history(symbol,`
- `field, n)`, `cross_section(field)`, `panel(fields, window)`, plus `chain(underlying, filters)` for listed contracts with quotes, IV and Greeks, `surface(underlying)` for the IV surface, and `contract(symbol)` for static terms. Out-of-range access raises instead of returning silently.

- Timing rule: the relation between signal time and fill time is set once in config and strategies cannot override it. For options, use fixed intraday snapshots: the signal at snapshot t sees completed daily bars plus the snapshot itself, never that day's close, and the fill uses a later quote at t plus a decision latency (for example signal at 15:45 ET, fill at 15:50 ET). Filling on the same quote the signal was computed from is a subtle form of look-ahead.

<a id="section-0-4"></a>
### 0.4 Error prevention

| Risk | Mechanism | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Look-ahead bias | DataView cuts at available_at; delay test | Data view, Research |
| Survivorship bias | Historical constituents, delisted and expired contracts included | Data |
| Bad data | Price jumps, zero volume, gaps, duplicate timestamps | Data validation |
| Stale or out-of-sync quotes | Option and underlying quotes must fall within a set time tolerance; stale quotes are flagged | Data validation |
| Mid-price fills | Buys fill at ask or worse, sells at bid or worse | Execution |
| Accounting errors | Invariant assertions on cash, positions, equity and daily P&L | Accounting |
| Illegal trades | Orders breaking trading hours, halts, position limits or borrow availability are rejected | Execution |
| Non-reproducibility | Fixed event order and random seeds; result hash comparison | Engine |
| Regressions | Golden strategies (buy-and-hold, equal- weight rebalance, a single long call held to expiry) locked | Tests and CI |

Invariants checked at minimum: cash ≥ 0 for non-margin accounts; position quantity equals cumulative fills; equity equals cash plus position value at the current multiplier; daily P&L equals equity change minus external flows; no open position in an expired contract.

<a id="section-0-5"></a>
### 0.5 Configuration and versioning

Four things uniquely define a run: strategy config (components and parameters), code commit, data snapshot ID and run settings (period, initial capital, cost model). Their hash forms the `run_id`.

Config is YAML, validated against a schema (for example pydantic) at load time. Unknown fields raise errors.

<a id="section-0-6"></a>
### 0.6 Logging and traceability

Every fill can be traced back through fill → order → target → signal → component, along with the data values used at the time (including the IV and Greeks at entry). Logs have three levels: decision log (on by default), full event stream (for debugging), and errors and warnings.

<a id="section-1"></a>
## Layer 1: Data

The data layer turns raw data into clean data that was truly available at time t. Most of a backtest's credibility is decided here, and for options most of the extra work is here too.

Pipeline: ingest → validate → clean → adjust → point-in-time alignment → IV and Greeks → surface → universe → features → storage and access.

| Submodule | Responsibility | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ingest | Pull raw data from sources | Underlying bars, option quotes, contract terms, corporate actions, index constituents, calendars, trading halts, earnings and event calendars, rates, dividends; incremental updates with retries; raw data is append-only |
| ContractMaster | Static terms of every contract | Underlying, call or put, strike, expiry, multiplier, exercise style, listing and delisting dates, full adjustment history |
| Quotes | Tradable prices | Option bid, ask and sizes at a fixed intraday snapshot plus volume, open interest and settlement price; the underlying quote at the same timestamp |
| Rates and dividends | Pricing inputs | Treasury or SOFR curve by tenor; discrete dividend schedule with ex-dates (needed to price American calls and judge early exercise); implied forwards from put-call parity, approximate for American options |
| Validate | Find problems, never fix them silently | Gaps, duplicate timestamps, OHLC contradictions, price jumps, zero volume; for options also stale quotes, crossed or locked markets, very wide spreads, prices below intrinsic value; a quality report per update |
| Clean | Apply explicit rules | Every rule configurable and logged; suspended or quote- less contracts are marked untradable, never forward-filled |
| Adjust | Corporate actions and contract adjustments | Store raw prices plus adjustment factors; signals use adjusted prices, fills and costs use raw prices; OCC contract adjustments (splits, special dividends, mergers, spin-offs) are applied by date; adjusted contracts with non-standard deliverables are flagged and excluded by default |
| PIT alignment | Data as of when it was known | Every record carries event_time and available_at; financials effective on announcement date; revisions versioned with as-of queries |
| IVCalculator and GreeksCalculator | One consistent pricing model | Solve IV from the mid price using the synchronized underlying, rate and dividend, with a European or American model matching the contract style (US equity and ETF options are American; index options such as SPX are European and cash-settled); one time convention (trading or calendar days) everywhere; compute delta, gamma, vega and theta; flag failures instead of guessing |
| SurfaceBuilder | IV surface per underlying | Grid by delta (or moneyness) × tenor; smoothing and arbitrage checks; derived features such as ATM IV, skew, term structure and IV rank |
| Universe | Tradable set per day | Underlyings: listing age, liquidity, exclusions. Options: the listed chain at t, filtered by days to expiry, moneyness, spread %, open interest. Expired and delisted contracts are kept in history |
| Features | Derived data | Dependency graph, cache keyed by parameter hash, incremental updates; features obey available_at like raw data |
| Store | Persistence and versions | Columnar files (for example Parquet) partitioned by date and underlying; a metadata DB for datasets, versions and snapshot IDs |
| Access | DataView for the layers above | history, `cross_section`, panel, chain, surface, contract; hot- data cache; a run binds to one data snapshot ID |

Four hard rules:

1. No data enters a backtest without an available_at.
2. Cleaning, adjustment and IV calculation are replayable: same raw data and rule version give the same result.
3. An option price and the underlying price used together must come from the same timestamp window.
4. Anything fitted (regime models, IV rank percentiles, surface smoothing, normalization statistics) is fitted only on data before t, using rolling or expanding windows. Regime models report filtered, not smoothed, probabilities, since smoothing uses future data.

<a id="section-2"></a>
## Layer 2: Signals

The signal layer answers what to buy or sell and how strongly. How much belongs to the portfolio layer, and whether it can fill belongs to execution.

The signal layer hosts most of the seven strategy components (see Strategy Model): Setup, Entry, Take Profit, Stop Loss, Headwind and position-level Hedge. It is stateful per trade: each component runs only in its lifecycle state, and all of them emit actions from the shared vocabulary. For options, an entry has two parts: a view on the underlying, then the choice of contracts that express it.

| Component | Strategy slot | Responsibility | Form |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| UniverseSelector | — | Pick candidate underlyings | Fixed list, index members, top N by a factor, rule-based screens |
| Filter | — | Drop what should not trade now | Liquidity, exclusions, data-quality gates |
| SetupRule | 1 Setup / Regime | Mark a candidate as ready or not | To be defined |
| EntryRule | 2 Entry | Fire the entry while the setup is valid | To be defined |
| ContractSelector | 2 Entry (if needed) | Turn the entry into specific contracts | To be defined |
| StructureBuilder | 2 Entry (if needed) | Define the legs | To be defined |
| TakeProfitRule | 3 Take Profit | Manage gains on an open trade | To be defined |
| StopLossRule | 4 Stop Loss | Manage losses on an open trade | To be defined |
| HeadwindRule | 5 Headwind | Respond to new adverse factors on an open trade | To be defined |
| PositionHedgeRule | 7 Hedge / Protection | Attach or remove protective legs on one trade | To be defined |
| RollRule | — | Replace legs with a later expiry or new strike | To be defined, optional |
| SignalCombiner | — | Merge actions issued in the same period | Applies the lifecycle's conflict policy (to be defined) |

<a id="section-2-1"></a>
### 2.1 Signal output

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| trade_id | The trade this action belongs to; main and hedge legs share it |
| action | One of the shared vocabulary: OPEN, ADD, REDUCE, CLOSE, ROLL, HEDGE_ADD, HEDGE_REMOVE, SET_STOP, HOLD |
| underlying | The underlying the trade is about |
| legs | Contract, side, ratio and role (main or hedge) for each leg |
| fraction | Share of the trade affected, for REDUCE |
| strength | Optional score or metadata passed on to Positioning |
| reason | What triggered it, with the data values used |
| component_id | The component and variant version that produced it |

<a id="section-2-2"></a>
### 2.2 Two interface styles

- Cross-sectional: score all candidates each period, as in multi-factor stock selection. Input is `cross_section`, output is a set of scored signals.
- Time-series: apply rules to one instrument, as in trend following. Input is history, output is that instrument's signal.

Most long-options strategies are time-series rules on the underlying, followed by a contract selector that queries chain. Both styles implement the same Component protocol, and the engine treats them alike.

<a id="section-2-3"></a>
### 2.3 Boundaries

- Exit, Headwind and Hedge components may read positions (entry premium, holding days, current Greeks, MFE and MAE so far) but never place orders.
- Per-trade decisions live here: stops, targets, headwinds and position-level hedges. Book-wide risk, including total premium, Greeks budgets, book-level headwinds and portfolio hedges, lives in Layer 3.

The full config example, organized by the seven components, is in the Strategy Model section.

<a id="section-3"></a>
## Layer 3: Portfolio and Risk

This layer turns signals into target positions and makes sure the portfolio stays within risk limits before any order goes out. Order of work: rebalance check → sizing → optimization (optional) → constraints → portfolio risk → target portfolio.

For a long-options book, the maximum loss on each position is the premium paid. So premium at risk is tracked as a core budget measure, and book risk is aggregated in Greeks. How individual trades are sized is the Positioning slot's job, and its form is not yet decided.

| Component | Strategy slot | Responsibility | Form |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RebalanceRule | — | Decide whether to act this period | Calendar, drift threshold, signal- driven |
| Sizer | 6 Positioning | Turn OPEN and ADD actions into contract quantities | To be defined |
| Optimizer | — | Best weights under constraints (optional) | Mean-variance, minimum variance, risk parity |
| RiskModel | — | Risk estimates for budgets and checks | Greeks aggregation by underlying and expiry bucket, plus beta- weighted delta and vega to a common index, because underlyings such as SPY, QQQ, IWM and their largest holdings are highly correlated; covariance and factor models for the underlyings |
| Constraint | — | Hard limits | Total premium outstanding, premium per underlying and per expiry, Greeks limits, minimum cash, contract position limits |
| RiskRule | 5 Headwind (book-wide) | Monitor and intervene on the whole book | Book-wide headwind responses to be defined; general limits such as drawdown breaker and daily loss limit |
| ScenarioRule | — | Stress the book | Revalue on a grid of spot moves, IV moves and time, with an explicit sticky-strike or sticky-delta assumption; block trades that breach a scenario loss limit |
| PortfolioHedgeRule | 7 Hedge / Protection (book-wide) | Protect the whole book | To be defined; hedge legs tagged with their own trade_id |

<a id="section-3-1"></a>
### 3.1 Risk actions

When a rule triggers it emits a RiskEvent. Actions are limited to a few kinds so they can be audited:

- Scale down: reduce all positions by a ratio.
- No new positions: only reductions allowed.
- Liquidate: close named contracts or the whole book.
- Pause strategy: until a person or a rule resumes it.

<a id="section-3-2"></a>
### 3.2 Output

TargetPortfolioEvent holds the target quantity for each contract plus the reason for every adjustment (which signal, which constraint cut it). Execution turns the gap between target and current positions into orders.

<a id="section-3-3"></a>
### 3.3 Who owns which risk

| Type | Examples | Layer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Per trade | 3 Take Profit, 4 Stop Loss, 5 Headwind on one position, 7 Hedge on one position, rolls | Layer 2 Signals |
| Portfolio | 6 Positioning, total premium, Greeks budgets, 5 Headwind on the whole book, 7 Hedge on the whole book, drawdown breaker, scenario limits | Layer 3 Portfolio and Risk |

<a id="section-4"></a>
## Layer 4: Execution Simulation

Execution decides how much of the target can fill and at what price. Its defaults should lean pessimistic: most of the gap between backtest and live comes from here, and for long options the single biggest source is filling at mid instead of paying the spread.

| Component | Responsibility | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OrderGenerator | Target − current → orders | Round to whole contracts; sell before buy so cash suffices; split large orders TWAP- or VWAP-style |
| OrderType | Order behavior | Market, limit, stop, opening or closing auction; DAY or GTC |
| MarketRule | Reject impossible orders | Trading hours (9:30 to 16:00 ET; some ETF and index options to 16:15), trading halts, Limit Up-Limit Down bands on the underlying, option tick sizes ($0.01 or $0.05 by price and program), position and exercise limits, short-sale borrow availability, T+1 settlement, the pattern day trader rule for small margin accounts |
| FillModel | Fill price and quantity | Options: buys fill at ask, sells at bid, on the configured snapshot; limit orders fill only when the price trades through; size capped by a participation rate of volume and by displayed size; unfilled remainder carries over or cancels |
| SlippageModel | Price beyond the quote | Options: a multiple of the half-spread, wider near expiry and for deep out-of-the-money strikes. Underlyings: fixed bps, half-spread, volatility-scaled, square-root impact |
| CostModel | Explicit fees | Options: per-contract commission plus exchange, ORF and OCC clearing fees, and SEC and FINRA TAF fees on sells. Stocks and ETFs: commission, SEC fee and FINRA TAF on sells, borrow fees on shorts. Also margin interest and funding costs |
| ExerciseModel | What happens at expiry | Close before expiry (default) or exercise; OCC exercise by exception at expiry (contracts $0.01 or more in the money are auto-exercised unless instructed otherwise); early exercise of American calls before ex-dividend dates; cash or margin needed to take delivery of shares; physical settlement for equity and ETF options, cash settlement (AM or PM) for index options, all into an ExpiryEvent |
| SimBroker | One interface for the outside | submit, cancel, on_snapshot; emits FillEvent and OrderStatusEvent; the live broker implements the same interface |

<a id="section-4-1"></a>
### 4.1 Option fill price

A buy fills at the mid price plus a multiple λ of the half-spread. λ = 1 means paying the full ask; test λ = 1.5 to see how much of the edge survives worse fills. Sells mirror this against the bid.

```
\text{fill}_{\text{buy}} = \text{mid} + \lambda \cdot (\text{ask} -
\text{mid}), \qquad \lambda \ge 1
```

For large trades in the underlying, the square-root impact model is a common starting point, where σ is daily volatility, Q is trade size, ADV is average daily volume and k is calibrated from live fills:

`\text{impact} = k \cdot \sigma \cdot \sqrt{\frac{Q}{\text{ADV}}}`

<a id="section-4-2"></a>
### 4.2 Suggested defaults

- Signal on snapshot t, fill on the quote at t plus the decision latency (for example 15:45 ET signal, 15:50 ET fill), always at bid or ask, never the close.

- Reject entries where the spread exceeds a set % of mid, or open interest is below a minimum.
- Participation cap: start at 5% to 10% of daily contract volume, then run a sensitivity test.
- Close positions before the final days to expiry unless exercise is part of the strategy. Log every rejected order and partial fill so research can report their share.

<a id="section-5"></a>
## Layer 5: Engine and Accounting

The engine drives events in the right order; accounting records every change in money exactly. Build them separately: scheduling can be complex, bookkeeping must be simple, testable and always correct.

<a id="section-5-1"></a>
### 5.1 Engine

| Component | Responsibility | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EventLoop | Dispatch events | Priority queue ordered by (timestamp, processing phase, sequence) so order is deterministic |
| Scheduler | Emit timed events | Start of day, snapshot time, rebalance days, end of day, expiry days, all from the trading and expiry calendars |
| Runner | Manage one run | Load config → bind data snapshot → build components → run → save results; state snapshots for resume |
| BatchRunner | Run many configs in parallel | Process pool or distributed (for example Ray); an independent random seed per task |
| VectorizedEngine | Fast screening during research | Matrix operations over all periods with simplified fills; useful for underlying-level signals only |

Event-driven is the primary mode for options. Contract selection, rolls and expiry are path-dependent, so vectorized results on option P&L are not trustworthy. Use the vectorized engine to screen views on the underlying, then validate in event-driven mode.

<a id="section-5-2"></a>
### 5.2 Accounting

| Component | Responsibility | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ledger | Record every money movement | Fills, fees, dividends, interest, exercise and expiry settlements, deposits and withdrawals; append-only |
| Positions | What is held | Keyed by contract and grouped by trade_id, each leg tagged main or hedge; quantity, multiplier, entry premium, open date, holding days, sellable quantity under the settlement rule |
| Cash | Cash state | Available, frozen by open orders, margin borrowed |
| Valuation | End-of-day mark-to- market | Long options marked at bid (conservative), mid also reported; underlyings at close; untradable contracts at last valid price, flagged |
| CorporateActions | Corporate events | Dividends to cash after tax; splits adjust quantity and cost; contract adjustments update multiplier and strike |
| Expiry | Settle expiring contracts | Exercise, cash settlement or lapse; removes the position and books the result |
| PnL | P&L breakdown | Realized, unrealized, fees, dividends; by contract, trade, leg role (main or hedge), the component that closed it, underlying and day |
| GreeksAttribution | Explain option P&L | Split daily P&L into delta, gamma, vega, theta and residual (see 5.3) |
| Snapshots | Data for research | Daily equity, cash, positions, premium at risk, net Greeks, turnover |

A TradeBook sits beside the ledger: one record per trade_id with its setup, entry, every action and the component that issued it, MFE and MAE in premium and underlying terms, and the final P&L split into main and hedge legs. After a trade closes, its contracts keep being tracked for a set window (shadow tracking), so research can compute post-exit MFE and counterfactual exits. Research reads trades from here.

At every end of day the engine runs the invariant checks from 0.4. If any fails, the run stops and dumps its state.

<a id="section-5-3"></a>
### 5.3 Greeks P&L attribution

Each position's daily value change is split using the Greeks from the start of the day, where S is the underlying price, σ is implied volatility and t is time:

```
\Delta V \approx \delta \, \Delta S + \tfrac{1}{2} \gamma \, (\Delta S)^2 +
\nu \, \Delta \sigma + \theta \, \Delta t + \varepsilon
```

A large residual ε points to bad data, a jump, or a model mismatch, and is worth investigating.

<a id="section-6"></a>
## Layer 6: Research and Reports

Research must answer whether a result is real, not just show a good-looking equity curve. Long-options strategies make this harder: they usually win rarely, earn most of their profit from a few large trades, and pay a persistent volatility risk premium.

| Component | Responsibility | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ExperimentTracker | Every run findable, comparable, reproducible | `run_id`, config, commit, data snapshot, summary results, tags; counts how many parameter sets were tried for one idea |
| ParamSweep | Explore parameters in bulk | Grid, random or Bayesian search; heatmaps show whether results sit on a stable plateau or an isolated spike |
| Validation | Detect overfitting | In-sample and out-of-sample split; walk-forward (rolling or expanding); purged k-fold; bootstrap of trades (important when trade count is small); one- bar signal delay; doubled costs and λ = 1.5 fills; results split by IV regime |
| Baselines | Separate skill from structure | Delta-equivalent position in the underlying (does the option add value?); random entries with the same structure, delta and days to expiry (does timing beat the volatility risk premium?) |
| Metrics | Quantify performance | See 6.1 |
| Attribution | Where returns come from | By contract, underlying and period; Greeks attribution (delta, gamma, vega, theta); contribution of each signal component |
| Report | Visual output | Equity vs benchmark, drawdowns, monthly returns heatmap, rolling Sharpe, net Greeks over time, premium at risk, IV at entry vs realized volatility, trade list; HTML or notebook export |
| Compare | Side-by-side results | Runs across parameters or versions; day-by-day backtest vs live gap analysis |

<a id="section-6-1"></a>
### 6.1 Metrics

| Category | Metrics |
| --- | --- |
| Return | Cumulative, annualized, excess; return on premium spent |
| Risk | Annualized volatility, downside volatility, max drawdown, drawdown duration and recovery |
| Risk-adjusted | Sharpe (read with care for skewed payoffs), Sortino, Calmar, information ratio, Deflated Sharpe |
| Trade | Win rate, payoff ratio, average holding period, share of profit from the top N trades, turnover, costs as a share of gross P&L, rejected and partial fills |
| Options | Theta paid, vega P&L, IV at entry vs realized volatility over the holding period, average spread paid as % of premium |
| Capacity | Participation distribution; return decay as capital grows |

<a id="section-6-2"></a>
### 6.2 Pre-launch checklist

- Out-of-sample performance does not collapse
- Results are stable around the chosen parameters
- Still works with signals delayed by one bar
- Still positive with doubled costs and λ = 1.5 fills
- Profit is not concentrated in a handful of trades or dates
- Beats the random-entry baseline with the same structure
- Greeks attribution matches the thesis (a directional strategy should earn mainly from delta)
- Total number of parameter sets tried is recorded

<a id="section-6-3"></a>
### 6.3 Component research

All seven strategy components are researched with the same tools, built once here and reused for every component:

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Ablation | Run the strategy with one slot switched off or filled by a neutral variant |
| Variant swap | Fill one slot with a different registered variant, everything else fixed |
| Slot sweep | Sweep one slot's parameters only, on the same trades where possible |
| Counterfactual exits | Replay each closed trade under an alternative exit to measure money saved or given up |
| Attribution by component | Split P&L by the slot whose action opened, sized, reduced, hedged or closed each part of a trade |
| Lifecycle settings | Compare Open-state run orders and conflict policies with all slots fixed |

Each comparison is a pair of runs differing in one component only, recorded in the ExperimentTracker so the history of every change to the strategy stays auditable.

Interaction tests cover dependencies between slots (see Component interactions): vary two slots jointly, for example Take Profit × Stop Loss or Headwind × Hedge, and compare the joint effect with the sum of the single-slot effects. A large gap means the two slots should be researched and tuned together.

<a id="section-6-4"></a>
### 6.4 Research protocol

Seven slots, each with variants and parameters, plus lifecycle settings, form a very large search space. With a low-frequency strategy that produces relatively few trades, the main risk is fitting history rather than finding an edge. These rules apply to all component research:

1. Lock a final hold-out period at the start and use it once, at the end.
2. Count every trial across all slots and settings in the ExperimentTracker; the Deflated Sharpe uses the total count.
3. Research in stages, each on walk-forward folds: Setup and Entry first, judged by forward returns of the underlying and of the selected options with no exits applied (event study); then Take Profit and Stop Loss; then Headwind; then Positioning; then Hedge. Finish with interaction tests and a joint re-check.
4. Report confidence intervals, not point estimates: bootstrap by trade and block bootstrap by period. Set a minimum trade count before any conclusion is drawn.
5. Pool trades across underlyings to gain sample size, but require the effect to hold on each underlying separately.
6. Counterfactual exit results are in-sample by construction; any change they suggest must be confirmed out-of-sample before adoption.
7. Compute return and risk metrics from daily mark-to-market P&L of the whole book, not from per-trade returns, so overlapping trades are counted correctly.

<a id="section-7"></a>
## Layer 7: Interfaces

The interface layer exposes the system to people and programs, and guarantees that backtest and live trading run the same strategy code with only the data feed and broker swapped.

| Component | Responsibility | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python SDK and CLI | Daily entry point for researchers | run, sweep, report, data update; callable from notebooks |
| REST API | Programmatic access | See 7.1 |
| JobQueue | Run backtests asynchronously | Submit, queue, progress, cancel, timeouts, resource quotas (for example Celery, RQ, Ray) |
| ResultStore | Keep results | Metadata in a relational DB (for example Postgres); equity, positions and fills in Parquet or object storage |
| Web UI | Visual operation | Strategy forms generated from parameter schemas, run list, reports, comparisons, data quality dashboard, IV surface and Greeks exposure views |
| LiveAdapter | Connect to real markets | Real-time underlying and option quote feeds, live broker implementing the SimBroker interface, paper trading, live vs simulated fill reconciliation, kill switch |
| Auth | Team use | Users and roles, strategy visibility, audit log |

## Directory Structure and Roadmap

Code directories map one-to-one to layers, and dependencies point only downward: an upper layer may import a lower one, never the reverse.

```

```

live/         feeds/  brokers/  reconcile.py

### Build order

1. Minimal loop: core events, components, clock and data view; daily underlying data; one entry and one exit rule; equal-weight sizing; next-open fills with a flat fee; accounting and basic metrics. Done when buy-and-hold matches a hand calculation.
2. Credibility: point-in-time data, delisted names, market rules, slippage and impact, invariant assertions, golden regression tests.
3. Options data and execution: contract master, bid and ask snapshots, rates and dividends, IV and Greeks, surface; contract selector and option exit rules; bid and ask fills, option market rules, expiry and exercise; Greeks attribution. Done when a single long call held to expiry matches a hand calculation, including fees and settlement.
4. Strategy components and research: trade lifecycle, action vocabulary, TradeBook, the seven component slots with a neutral variant each, ablation and counterfactual tools; feature cache, vectorized screening, parameter sweeps, walk-forward, baselines, experiment tracking, reports.
5. Portfolio: premium and Greeks budgets, scenario limits, rolls, optional optimizer.
6. Platform: REST API, job queue, web UI.
7. Live: real-time feeds, broker adapter, paper trading, reconciliation.

Credibility and options execution come before research speed, because running faster on an engine you cannot trust produces conclusions you cannot use.

## Research and Trade-off Register

Every choice in the system that can be researched or involves a trade-off falls into one of four groups, and the groups are treated differently. Realism assumptions (group 1) are set conservatively and only tested for sensitivity: picking the value that maximizes backtest returns would optimize an illusion. Strategy and research choices (groups 3 and 4) can be optimized, but only under the research protocol in 6.4.

### 1. Realism assumptions: sensitivity tests only, never optimized

| Choice | Trade-off | How to test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fill price multiple λ (where between mid and ask a buy fills) | Closer to mid gives higher returns but less realism | Run λ = 0.5, 1 and 1.5; the strategy must hold at λ = 1 or worse |
| Decision latency | Longer is more conservative but may understate what is achievable | Run several latencies (for example 1, 5, 15 minutes) and check how fast returns decay |
| Participation cap | A higher cap means more capacity but less realism | Returns and capacity at several caps |
| Mark-to-market at bid or mid | Bid inflates drawdowns and can trigger premium-based stops on spread noise; mid is noisier | Run both and compare stop triggers and drawdowns |
| Stale-quote tolerance | Stricter rules give cleaner data but fewer usable observations | Several thresholds; conclusions should not change |
| Data-cleaning rules (for example dropping wide- spread days) | Cleaner data, but may remove stressed periods and bias results toward calm markets | Compare results with and without, focusing on stress periods |
| Excluding OCC-adjusted contracts | Avoids pricing errors but loses data | Report the share and timing of excluded contracts |
| American vs European IV model | European is faster; American is accurate for equity and ETF options | Compare IV and Greeks on a sample |
| Trading-day vs calendar-day time | Changes weekend and holiday theta and IV levels | Pick one everywhere; check Monday P&L attribution |
| Dividend and rate sources | Forecast vs implied from put-call parity | Compare the effect on in- the-money call pricing |
| Surface smoothing | More smoothing means less noise but more bias | Check whether smoothed features change Setup decisions |
| Sticky-strike vs sticky-delta scenarios | The two give different scenario losses | Compute both; risk limits use the more conservative |
| Greeks attribution method (start-of-period vs averaged Greeks) | Different methods leave different residuals | Compare residual size and stability |

### 2. Engineering trade-offs

| Choice | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| Data granularity (daily close vs intraday snapshots) | Cost and storage vs realism; decides how realistic much of the rest can be |
| check_frequency for Open-state slots | Faster reaction vs more noise and turnover; must equal live trading |
| Event-driven vs vectorized engine | Accuracy vs speed; vectorized only for underlying-level screening |
| Underlying universe (index ETFs only vs single stocks) | More trades vs earnings events, wider spreads, borrow constraints and more data |
| Shadow-tracking window after exit | Fuller counterfactual analysis vs storage and compute |

### 3. Strategy choices to research

| Choice | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| Signal snapshot time | More information closer to the close vs less time before the fill |
| Contract delta and days to expiry | Leverage and convexity vs theta decay, IV cost and liquidity |
| Structure (single leg, straddle, spread) | Convexity vs cost; spreads cap upside and need margin |
| Take Profit approach | Locking in gains vs keeping the tail; much of a long option's value is in the tail, so tight targets erode convexity |
| Stop Loss on premium vs on the underlying | Premium stops react to IV and spread noise; underlying stops follow the thesis but leave the maximum loss open |
| Headwind sensitivity | Over-reaction (false alarms, extra costs) vs under-reaction |
| Hedge approach and instruments | Protection vs cost, capped upside and basis risk |
| Rolling | Keeping exposure vs paying the spread again |
| Positioning (premium budget, scaling in) | Return vs drawdown; scaling in vs entering at once |
| Regime model | Fast models whipsaw, stable ones lag; more regimes leave fewer samples per regime |
| Lifecycle settings (run order, conflict policy, concurrency, re-entry) | Each changes strategy behavior and is researched like a component |
| Book limits (total premium, Greeks caps) | Risk vs opportunity |

### 4. Research-method trade-offs

| Choice | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| Walk-forward window length | Short windows adapt but estimate noisily; long windows the reverse |
| Hold-out length | More test data means less research data |
| Pooling across underlyings | Sample size vs differences between underlyings |
| Number of variants tested | More chances to find a good result vs a larger multiple-testing penalty |
| Optimization objective | Sharpe penalizes convex payoffs; use Sortino, tail metrics and return on premium alongside it |
| Minimum trade count and bootstrap block length | Stricter thresholds give more reliable but fewer conclusions |

### Priorities

For a long-options strategy, five items move results most and should be studied first: λ, decision latency and mark-to-market method from group 1, and contract choice and Take Profit approach from group 3.

## Quant Review Notes

A review from a quant research perspective found thirteen issues. All are now handled structurally in this document; six decisions remain open and are listed at the end.

| Issue | Why it matters | Resolution | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Signal and fill on the same quote | Subtle look-ahead that overstates entry and exit prices | Signal at snapshot t, fill at t plus a decision latency; signals never see that day's close | 0.3, 4.2 |
| Stops and targets between snapshots | With snapshot data, the order of a stop and a target hit within one period is unknown | Open-state slots run only at check_frequency, identical to live | Lifecycle settings |
| Regime models fitted on full history | Smoothed regime probabilities and full- sample percentiles use future data | Fit only on data before t; filtered probabilities | Layer 1, rule 4 |
| Setups vs trades unclear | Concurrent trades and re-entry were undefined | Candidate (per underlying) and trade (per trade_id) scopes; concurrency and re-entry settings | Lifecycle states |
| Large search space | Seven slots with variants invite false discoveries | Staged research, trial counting, Deflated Sharpe, locked hold-out | 6.4 |
| Small, skewed samples | Low-frequency long options give few trades with fat-tailed payoffs | Bootstrap confidence intervals, minimum trade count, pooled but per- underlying checks | 6.4 |
| Counterfactual exits lack data | Without prices after exit, stop and target research is guesswork | Shadow tracking of closed contracts | 5.2 |
| Correlated underlyings | SPY, QQQ, IWM and their largest holdings behave largely like one position | Beta-weighted delta and vega to a common index | Layer 3 RiskModel |
| American exercise and dividends | US equity and ETF options are American; a long call can be worth exercising before an ex-dividend date, and ignoring this misstates P&L and expiry handling | Discrete dividend schedule in the data layer; American exercise logic in ExerciseModel; American pricing model for IV | Layers 1 and 4 |
| Inconsistent IV models | Model or time- convention mismatches distort Greeks and attribution | One model per contract style, one time convention, stated sticky assumption | Layers 1 and 3 |
| Metrics on overlapping trades | Per-trade returns misstate book risk | Metrics from daily book mark-to-market P&L | 6.4 |
| Adjusted contracts | After splits, special dividends or mergers, OCC-adjusted contracts deliver non-standard baskets; their prices and Greeks no longer match standard pricing | Contract master tracks adjustments; adjusted contracts flagged and excluded by default | Layer 1 |
| Earnings and scheduled events | Single-stock options carry an IV run-up before earnings and a sharp IV drop after; long options held through an event behave very differently | Point-in-time earnings and event calendar in the data layer, readable by Setup, Entry and Headwind; results split by event exposure | Layer 1, Strategy Model, 6.4 |

### Open decisions

| Decision | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Historical option quote granularity | Intraday bid and ask snapshots are needed for the timing rules; with daily close data only, fills must be modeled more pessimistically and the bias stated |
| Signal snapshot time and fill latency | Sets how realistic entries and exits are; must match how orders will be placed live |
| check_frequency for Open-state slots | Determines how quickly stops, targets and headwinds can react, in backtest and live alike |
| Hold-out period and minimum trade count | Defines when a research result is allowed to count |
| Hedge instruments | Underlying shares, index futures (ES, MES), options, or a mix; decides what Layers 4 and 5 must support |
| Underlying universe | Index ETFs only, or single stocks too; single stocks add earnings handling, many more contracts, wider spreads and borrow constraints |
